source.title: Do Thinking Tokens Help with Safety?
source.authors: Narutatsu Ri; Abhishek Panigrahi; Sanjeev Arora

page_placements.theme: Early signals and commitment windows support safety monitoring

record.tranche_reason: Extends the study of early refusal/compliance signals to reasoning models, using hidden-state separability and probes rather than the original studies’ fine-tuning or aligned/base per-token KL measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper reports first-token refusal/compliance predictability and position-wise Fisher separability, but does not measure aligned/base per-token KL, harmful or benign safety-eroding fine-tuning, compliant-opening prefills, suffix attacks, or decoding changes of the kind named in the claim. Its inference-time and training-based safety defenses are not equivalent to the claimed bypass or safety-eroding fine-tuning interventions.
record.test_reason: The study probes reasoning models' hidden states and finds the final refusal/compliance outcome is linearly decodable at the first thinking token. It also finds that short thinking prefixes lock in the outcome. It does not measure aligned-vs-base per-token KL (V3), harmful or benign fine-tuning erosion (V1, V2), compliant-prefill, suffix or decoding bypasses (V4), weight localization (V5), causes of shallowness (V6), or training that deepens safety beyond the first tokens (V7). It cites Qi et al. and frames its results as extending shallow alignment to reasoning models, but its measures are related constructs: separability of refusal vs compliance, continuation variance, and defense ASR/ORR tradeoffs. The safety defenses it evaluates are not deepening methods in V7's sense. The reader's 'tests/T3' is therefore downgraded.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct, but incomplete. The authors also conclude that thinking acts as prefix completion rather than deliberative revision. Enabling thinking does not improve both ASR and ORR at once, and most text-level oscillations do not shift the final outcome. They also find that inference- and training-based defenses mainly trade ASR for ORR. Inference-time defenses and on-policy training suppress oscillations. Off-policy training (STAR-1, SafeKey) instead lowers first-token readability (AUROC −0.11) while largely preserving meaningful oscillations.
record.recipe_differences: Uses hidden-state Fisher separability and logistic probes on reasoning models, not the original studies’ fine-tuning interventions or aligned/base per-token KL measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: Position within the thinking trace changes Fisher separability: it is high at the first position, falls through the trace, and rises again near its end. Probe performance also differs between hidden representations and first-token text controls.

fits_no_version.finding: A linear probe on the first thinking-token hidden state predicts the final refusal/compliance label (AUROC 0.84–0.95). A TF-IDF probe on the first token is near chance, except partially for GPT-OSS-20B and Phi-4 on harmful prompts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In reasoning models, the final refusal/compliance decision is linearly decodable from the first thinking-token representation before any visible reasoning.

fits_no_version.finding: Fisher separability between eventual-refusal and eventual-compliance traces is U-shaped over thinking position in the four primary models. Five supplementary models (Qwen3-32B, Qwen3.5-9B, Phi-4-Reasoning-Plus, two DeepSeek-R1 distills) show the same pattern (Fig. 7; no rows).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal/compliance separability in reasoning models peaks at the start and end of the thinking trace.

fits_no_version.finding: With a fixed thinking prefix of only 20% of the trace, continuation variance of the refusal outcome is below 0.2, far under the fair-coin reference of 0.875 (Fig. 3). Thinking vs no-think leaves 70–97% of majority labels unchanged. 71–92% of stance oscillations are performative (Fig. 4, 5). No rows record these results, and rows_left_out does not declare them.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In reasoning models, an early thinking prefix fixes the refusal/compliance outcome; later thinking rarely changes it.

fits_no_version.finding: The probe readout is weak through most of the prompt prefill and spikes near the end of prefill (Fig. 2; no rows).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal/compliance decisions consolidate at the end of prompt prefill in reasoning models.

record.problems: The primary evidence is for probe predictability and Fisher separability, not a direct measurement of aligned-versus-base per-token KL or a causal account of safety behavior. Several position-wise Fisher results are presented as plots without tabulated values. The authors state that the study covers open-weight reasoning models of moderate sizes and refusal/compliance on selected harmful and benign prompt sets.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted inference- and training-defense ASR/ORR tables, defense oscillation counts, and thinking-budget comparisons: these do not test the listed fine-tuning erosion or compliant-opening bypass conditions, and the training defenses deliberately target safety reasoning. Their results are summarized in the authors’ conclusion and gate_note.

untested.parts: No harmful fine-tuning attack is run; the training studied is safety defenses.
No benign fine-tuning erosion is measured. Defense training on mixed safety and benign data is not ordinary benign fine-tuning.
No aligned-vs-base per-token KL. The study measures refusal-vs-compliance separability within one model.
No compliant prefill, adversarial suffix or decoding attack. SafePath's safety primer is a defense prefix, not a bypass.
No test of data or objective as the cause. The authors list the origin of the early signal as future work.
No method aimed at spreading safety beyond the first tokens. The defenses evaluated (STAR-1, SafeKey, R1-ACT, ThinkSafe, STAIR, RAPO) target safety reasoning in general.

record.verdict_notes: The paper explicitly positions itself as extending shallow safety alignment (Qi et al.) to reasoning models. However, its measures concern within-model predictability of the outcome, not aligned-vs-base divergence or bypass attacks, so none of V1–V7 is directly tested. A researcher might treat its first-token readout and prefix-locking results as analogous evidence for V3 or V4 in reasoning models. This record keeps them under fits_no_version. No instructions were found in the text.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a few to a few hundred harmful examples make a safety-trained model comply.
Whether ordinary or carefully chosen benign data raises harmful compliance.
The aligned-versus-base per-token KL divergence on harmful prompts; the paper instead measures refusal/compliance separability and probe performance.
Whether a compliant opening, adversarial suffix, or decoding change bypasses refusal.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
Whether the data or training objective causes safety shallowness.
Whether training that spreads safety beyond the first tokens does so, and whether it holds up.

relation.reason: The introduction, discussion and Appendix A explicitly relate the findings to shallow safety alignment, without directly testing or using a specified version.

tranche.reason: First-token decodability and stability under thinking-prefix continuation measure a related construct, rather than any specified claim version. The study does not measure aligned/base KL concentration, refusal bypass, parameter localization, fine-tuning erosion, the training origin of shallowness, or training that spreads safety beyond opening tokens.

source_check.notes: The stated AUROC range summarizes separate harmful/benign pools (0.840–0.948); pooled Qwen3-8B reaches 0.971. Row states describe probe predictivity, not evidence for V1–V7.
